body.p: Claims 1-20 are pending in the present application. Independent claims 1, 11 and 20 were amended in this response, along with dependent claims 8 and 18. No new matter was introduced as a result of the amendments. Support for the amendments may be found, for example, in 110020- 0028 and 0036 of the present specification. Entry of the amendments and favorable reconsideration are earnestly requested.

Claims 8 and 18 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. §112(d) as being of improper dependent form for failing to further limit the subject matter of the claim upon which it depends, or for failing to include all the limitations of the claim upon which it depends. In light of the present amendments to claims 8 and 18, Applicant submits the rejection is overcome. Withdrawal of the rejection is earnestly requested.
Claims 1-9, 11-18 and 20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Takeya (US Pat. Pub. No. 2022/0017056) in view of Inoue et al. (US Pat. Pub. No. 2009/0025996); and

Claims 10 and 19 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Takeya (US Pat. Pub. No. 2022/0017056) in view of Inoue et al. (US Pat. Pub. No. 2009/0025996), and further in view of Kelly (US Pat. Pub. No. 2017/0043778). Applicant submits the rejections are improper and should be withdrawn.
Specifically, neither Takeya nor Inoue teach or suggest the features of amended independent claim 1, highlighted below:
1. A method for restrained movement of a vehicle comprising
a drive unit for accelerating the vehicle, and a braking unit for
braking the vehicle, comprising:
actively generating a restraining drive torque via the drive unit to counteract an applied braking torque and facilitate
controlled vehicle movement during maneuvering operations;
applying and adjusting the braking torque, via the braking unit, to maintain the restraining drive torque, wherein the
restraining drive torque and braking torque are continuously
and dynamically modulated during maneuvering operations to
regulate vehicle positioning; and
braking the vehicle by reducing the restraining drive torque while maintaining a braking torque; and
reducing the restraining torque during the maneuvering operations by dynamically reducing the braking torque and
the restraining drive torque, wherein the braking torque is reduced with a smaller torque reduction gradient than the
restraining drive torque while the vehicle is actively
maneuvering.
Takeya describes a system for maintaining vehicle speed by balancing a driving force and
a braking force. The Examiner cites 10046 of Takeya, which states:

A vehicle control device includes a driving force control unit (not illustrated) that controls a driving force generated by a wheel of a vehicle, and a braking force control unit (ESC-ECU 8, EPB-ECU 9) that controls a braking force generated by the wheel. In the first embodiment, the vehicle control device controls the speed of the vehicle to be constant by the driving force control unit generating a driving force of a first prescribed amount and the braking force control unit generating a braking force of a second prescribed
amount.
Takeya further states that:

The vehicle control device can make the speed of the vehicle constant by controlling the driving force and the braking force so as to balance each other, and can realize both acceleration and deceleration by dynamically controlling one of the driving force and
the braking force from this state.

Takeya does not disclose "actively generating a restraining drive torque via the drive unit to counteract an applied braking torque and facilitate controlled vehicle movement during maneuvering operations." The cited portion of Takeya describes a system for maintaining a

constant speed, where braking and driving forces are balanced rather than a system where a restraining drive torque is actively generated to counteract braking torque. The explicit claim language recites that the restraining drive torque is actively generated and is applied to counteract braking torque. Takeya does not describe an active counteraction between braking and driving forces, as it merely discusses a control system that keeps speed constant by adjusting either force as needed. Takeya does not describe or suggest generating a drive torque specifically to counteract

an applied braking torque. Instead, Takeya describes balancing braking and driving forces to maintain speed, rather than using drive torque as an opposing force to braking torque as explicitly recited in the claim.

The Examiner asserts that Takeya discloses applying and adjusting the braking torque, via the braking unit, to maintain the restraining drive torque, wherein the restraining drive torque and braking torque are continuously and dynamically modulated during maneuvering operations to regulate vehicle positioning. The Examiner cites 0046 and Figure 3 to support this contention. However, Takeya does not describe continuously and dynamically modulating both braking torque and restraining drive torque during maneuvering operations. Figure 3 of Takeya shows that the driving force is held constant in certain time periods while braking force is adjusted, and vice versa. Takeya states in 0054:

After time t14, the vehicle can be accelerated in a time zone in which the driving force is larger than the braking force, and the vehicle can be decelerated in a time zone in which the driving force is smaller than the braking force by dynamically controlling the braking force
while keeping the driving force fixed.

This disclosure confirms that Takeya does not describe or suggest continuously and dynamically modulating both the braking torque and restraining drive torque during maneuvering operations to regulate vehicle positioning. The cited disclosure explicitly states that only one of the two forces is varied at a time, meaning Takeya does not teach simultaneous modulation of both forces as explicitly recited in the claim.

Inoue is cited to allegedly disclose reducing the restraining torque during the maneuvering operations by dynamically reducing the braking torque and the restraining drive torque, wherein the braking torque is reduced with a smaller torque reduction gradient than the restraining drive torque while the vehicle is actively maneuvering. The Examiner relies on 0 192 of Inoue, which states:

In addition, the vehicle braking force is reduced gradually toward the vehicle driving force corresponding to the amount of braking operation performed by the driver at a braking force reduction rate which is always lower than the driving force reduction rate. In other words, the vehicle braking force is reduced gently in such a manner that the amount of decrease in the vehicle braking force is always
smaller than the amount of decrease in the vehicle driving force.

This disclosure does not describe reducing the restraining torque during the maneuvering operations. Instead, Inoue describes a stopping process where the driving force is gradually reduced to zero, and then braking force is gradually decreased. The claim explicitly recites reducing the restraining torque while the vehicle is actively maneuvering, not while it is stopping. Inoue's disclosure describes a sequential stopping process, where the vehicle's driving force is reduced to zero before the braking force is reduced, rather than a method in which both forces are actively and dynamically reduced during maneuvering operations.

The explicit claim language recites that braking torque and restraining drive torque are reduced dynamically while the vehicle is actively maneuvering. In contrast, 0192 of Inoue describes a process where the driving force is first reduced to zero before the braking force is reduced. A PHOSITA would immediately recognize that this process does not meet the explicit claim language, as it describes a controlled stopping mechanism rather than a method for maneuvering operations.

Additionally, the Examiner states that Takeya and Inoue can be combined because Inoue teaches maintaining speed through simultaneous application of braking and drive torques. The Examiner cites 0003 of Inoue, which states: "The present invention relates to a vehicle control device that controls the vehicle driving force and vehicle braking force to be applied to a vehicle to maintain the vehicle body speed (vehicle speed) at a target vehicle speed."

This disclosure does not describe a system that dynamically reduces braking torque and restraining drive torque while the vehicle is actively maneuvering. 0003 of Inoue is a broad introductory statement describing general speed control principles. The Examiner has not cited any portion of Inoue that describes dynamically reducing both braking and drive torque during maneuvering operations as explicitly required by the claim.

The combination of Takeya and Inoue does not disclose or suggest the explicit claim limitations under a broadest reasonable interpretation. Takeya describes a system for maintaining constant speed, where either the braking force or driving force is adjusted individually. Takeya does not disclose actively generating a restraining drive torque to counteract an applied braking torque. Inoue describes a sequential stopping process, where the driving force is reduced to zero before braking force is reduced, rather than dynamically adjusting both forces while the vehicle is

actively maneuvering. A PHOSITA would immediately recognize that these systems operate fundamentally differently from the claimed method. The proposed combination does not result in predictable results because Takeya's constant speed maintenance and Inoue's sequential stopping method do not logically integrate into a system where restraining drive torque and braking torque are continuously and dynamically modulated during maneuvering operations to regulate vehicle positioning.

Because neither Takeya nor Inoue discloses or suggests the explicit claim limitations, and because a PHOSITA would not reasonably modify Takeya's system with Inoue's sequential stopping method, the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103 should be withdrawn.

Furthermore, there is no apparent reason why a PHOSITA would combine Takeya with Inoue in the manner suggested, as the proposed combination of Takeya and Inoue does not logically result in the claimed method, and the rationale for combination is flawed under MPEP § 2143.01 and MPEP § 2143.02.

Takeya describes a system that maintains a constant speed by adjusting either the braking force or the driving force individually (Takeya 0046: "Both acceleration and deceleration controllable by performing one of the control of the driving force by the driving force control unit and the control of the braking force by the braking force control unit."). The Examiner has acknowledged that Takeya does not explicitly disclose braking the vehicle by reducing the restraining drive torque or reducing the restraining torque by reducing the braking torque and the restraining drive torque, wherein the braking torque is reduced with a smaller torque reduction gradient than the restraining drive torque during braking (Advisory Action). The Examiner instead relies on Inoue to allegedly provide these features. However, Inoue describes a sequential stopping process, where the driving force is reduced to zero before the braking force is reduced (Inoue 0190: "The CPU gradually reduces the driving force request value EGReqTqC ... The vehicle driving force reaches '0' at a time t2.").

This is fundamentally different from the explicit claim language, which requires continuously and dynamically modulating both torques during maneuvering operations to regulate vehicle positioning. Inoue's approach is incompatible with the claimed method because it does not involve maintaining a restraining drive torque while braking but rather eliminates driving force altogether before reducing braking force (Inoue 0192: "The vehicle braking force is reduced
gradually ... at a braking force reduction rate which is always lower than the driving force reduction rate.").

The Examiner's stated rationale for combining Takeya and Inoue is that doing so would allow the system to "more gradually come to a stop and prevent uncomfortable lurching." However, this reasoning fails under MPEP § 2143.01, which requires a reasonable expectation of success in combining the references. MPEP § 2143.01 states: "For a conclusion of obviousness to be appropriate, there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness. Rejections on obviousness grounds cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; instead, there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness."

Takeya and Inoue describe fundamentally different control methodologies: Takeya's system balances forces to maintain a constant speed, while Inoue's system reduces forces sequentially to bring the vehicle to a stop. A PHOSITA would recognize that these two control strategies are incompatible without significant redesign. The Examiner cites Inoue 0196, which states that "the vehicle driving force... is prevented from becoming excessive relative to the vehicle braking force as a second force." However, this passage does not teach or suggest continuously and dynamically modulating both torques to regulate vehicle positioning during maneuvering operations. Rather, it describes preventing excessive driving force relative to braking force, which is a different concept.

Furthermore, MPEP § 2143.03 makes clear that all claim limitations must be considered when determining patentability. MPEP § 2143.03 states: "Any inquiry into the obviousness of the invention requires consideration of all the limitations of the claims. The examiner must show that each and every limitation is disclosed in the applied prior art or would have been obvious in view of the applied prior art."

The Examiner's analysis does not take into account the explicit claim requirement that restraining drive torque and braking torque are "continuously and dynamically modulated during maneuvering operations to regulate vehicle positioning." Neither Takeya nor Inoue discloses or suggests this feature. Takeya's system adjusts forces to maintain constant speed (Takeya 0049: "The vehicle body speed can be made constant by balancing the driving force and the braking force."), and Inoue's system reduces forces sequentially during stopping (Inoue 0190: "The

vehicle driving force reaches '0' at a time t2."). Neither reference describes a control strategy where braking torque and restraining drive torque are dynamically adjusted together to control vehicle movement.

Additionally, the Examiner's combination violates MPEP § 2143.01 because it does not yield predictable results. MPEP § 2143.01 states: "Obviousness can only be established by combining or modifying the teachings of the prior art to produce the claimed invention where there is some teaching, suggestion, or motivation to do so found either explicitly or implicitly in the references themselves, or within the knowledge generally available to one of ordinary skill in the art."

The Examiner asserts that combining Takeya's speed maintenance system with Inoue's stopping system would produce a predictable result. However, a PHOSITA would recognize that Takeya's system relies on fixed balancing of forces, while Inoue's system eliminates drive force before reducing braking force. These are conflicting control methodologies that do not integrate seamlessly. The Examiner has not explained how one of ordinary skill in the art would modify Takeya's constant-speed approach to incorporate Inoue's sequential stopping method while still achieving the claimed "continuous and dynamic modulation of forces." Without such an explanation, the rejection lacks the required rational underpinning.

Moreover, the Examiner's reliance on an "obvious to try" rationale is improper under MPEP § 2143.01. MPEP § 2143.01 states: "An 'obvious to try' rationale is only appropriate when there is a finite number of identified, predictable solutions and a PHOSITA would have a reasonable expectation of success in pursuing these known options."

The Examiner suggests that modifying Takeya with Inoue would have been an obvious design choice to prevent uncomfortable lurching. However, an obvious-to-try rationale is only applicable when a PHOSITA has a limited number of predictable solutions to choose from. Here, the proposed modification requires fundamentally changing how Takeya's system operates, and there is no indication in the prior art that such a modification would work without undue experimentation. The Examiner has not provided evidence that a PHOSITA would have considered this combination predictable or viable.
In conclusion, the Examiner's rejection fails to meet the requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 103. The references do not disclose or suggest the explicit features recited in the claims, and the
rationale for combining the references is speculative and unsupported. For these reasons, the rejection of claim 1 should be withdrawn.

For at least these reasons, Applicant submits the rejection to independent claim 1 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 is overcome and should be withdrawn. As amended independent claims 11 and 20 recite similar features, they are allowable for the same reasons. The remining dependent claims are allowable by virtue of their dependence upon their respective base claims.

In light of the present amendment and arguments, Applicants respectfully submit that the patent application is in condition for allowance and request an early Notice of Allowance.
